lessons.title: Mayflower Compact
lessons.deck: A temporary agreement for civil government, written because the passengers reached Cape Cod outside the territory covered by their original patent.

facts.label: Place
facts.value: Aboard ship in Cape Cod Harbor

sections.heading: Why it was written
paragraphs: The passengers intended to settle under a Virginia Company patent somewhere south of Long Island Sound. Storms and navigation instead brought them to Cape Cod, north of the patent's authority. Some non-Separatist passengers reportedly argued that nobody could command them once they landed outside the authorized territory. Before anyone went ashore, the adult men created an agreement that would hold the community together until a new patent arrived.

The passengers are often divided into Saints and Strangers. The Saints were members of the English Separatist congregation that had lived in Leiden in the Dutch Republic. The Strangers were other passengers recruited for the venture, including servants, craftsmen, and people seeking economic opportunity. The agreement joined both groups under one civil government without erasing their religious differences.

sections.heading: What the text did
paragraphs: The signers declared themselves loyal subjects of King James and said their voyage served God, the Christian faith, king, and country. They then covenanted together into a civil body politic. That body could enact just and equal laws, ordinances, acts, constitutions, and offices for the general good, and the signers promised submission and obedience.

This was not a declaration of independence, a modern constitution, or a guarantee of universal democracy. It was a short governing covenant among forty-one of the fifty adult men aboard; women and children did not sign. Its immediate purpose was order and legal continuity. John Carver appears first on the traditional signer list and became the settlement's first governor. William Brewster is often identified as the likely drafter, but the authorship is not certain.

sections.heading: How the text survived
paragraphs: The original document is lost. The earliest surviving text appears in Mourt's Relation, published in London in 1622 and principally written by Edward Winslow and William Bradford. Bradford later copied it into Of Plymouth Plantation. Samuel Purchas printed another early version in 1625, while Nathaniel Morton supplied the familiar signer list in New-England's Memorial in 1669.

The agreement was a stopgap because the group lacked valid authority at Cape Cod. A new patent obtained through John Peirce supplied a firmer legal basis in 1621. The document nevertheless became a retrospective symbol of government by consent; John Quincy Adams later praised it as an example of the social compact imagined by political philosophers.

lessons.title: Plymouth Colony
lessons.deck: The smaller Pilgrim settlement at Patuxet: Bradford, Winslow, Standish, Wampanoag diplomacy, the 1621 harvest gathering, and eventual absorption into a royal province.

sections.heading: Arrival at Patuxet
paragraphs: The English Separatists remembered as Pilgrims had left England for Leiden before arranging a transatlantic venture financed by the Merchant Adventurers. Their ship reached Cape Cod in November 1620. After exploring the coast, the settlers chose Patuxet, a Wampanoag village emptied by an epidemic, and began building in December. This was not the first permanent English settlement; Jamestown had existed since 1607.

The first winter was catastrophic. Disease and exposure killed roughly half the settlers. John Carver, selected as the first governor, died in April 1621. William Bradford succeeded him and was elected governor about thirty times over the next three decades. Edward Winslow and Thomas Prence also repeatedly held the office, while Myles Standish served as the principal military commander.

sections.heading: Wampanoag relations and the harvest gathering
paragraphs: Samoset, an Abenaki visitor who knew some English, made the first recorded greeting. Tisquantum, usually called Squanto, was Patuxet. He had learned English after being kidnapped by Thomas Hunt, sold in Spain, and living in England before returning home. He interpreted and advised the settlers, but his diplomacy pursued his own position among Native communities rather than simple friendship.

In March 1621, the settlers made a mutual-defense agreement with the Wampanoag sachem Ousamequin, commonly called Massasoit. Edward Winslow became a central diplomat. In autumn 1621, Massasoit and about ninety Wampanoag men joined a three-day harvest gathering. Winslow's account in Mourt's Relation is the only contemporary eyewitness description; the event acquired the label First Thanksgiving much later.

sections.heading: Government, conflict, and the end
paragraphs: The Mayflower Compact supplied the first civil agreement, while the governor and General Court developed a working government. A 1636 codification gathered laws for the settlement. The arrival of the Fortune in 1621 and Little James in 1623 increased the population. In 1623, leaders shifted crop production from a common arrangement to family plots, improving incentives without creating a simple modern free-market system.

The settlement joined the New England Confederation in 1643 with Massachusetts Bay, Connecticut, and New Haven. Its forces participated in the Pequot War. Relations with the Wampanoag collapsed after Massasoit's death, the suspicious death of his son Wamsutta, and the murder of interpreter John Sassamon. King Philip's War began in this jurisdiction in 1675 under Metacom, Massasoit's son. A 1691 royal charter combined this settlement with Massachusetts Bay, Maine, and other territory in the Province of Massachusetts Bay, effective in 1692.

lessons.title: Massachusetts Bay Colony
lessons.deck: The chartered Puritan polity centered on Boston: company government, Winthrop's migration, representative institutions, dissent, law, and royal consolidation.

sections.heading: Company becomes government
paragraphs: The failed Dorchester Company settlement at Cape Ann preceded a new effort. John Endecott led settlers to Naumkeag, renamed Salem, in 1628. The New England Company received a land grant, and Charles I issued a royal charter to the Massachusetts Bay Company in 1629. Matthew Cradock served as the company's first governor in England but never lived in New England.

The unusual Cambridge Agreement of 1629 promised that investors would move to New England if the charter and company government went with them. John Winthrop was elected governor, and the Winthrop Fleet carried roughly seven hundred migrants on eleven ships in 1630. Winthrop sailed on the Arbella and delivered A Model of Christian Charity, warning that their community would be watched as a city upon a hill. Boston replaced water-poor Charlestown as the political center.

sections.heading: A Puritan commonwealth
paragraphs: These settlers were Puritans who generally hoped to reform the Church of England, not the Separatists associated with Plymouth. In 1631, full political freemanship was restricted to male members of approved churches. The General Court originally resembled a company meeting, but towns began sending elected deputies in 1634. The government combined corporate charter, representative practices, and a religiously restricted electorate.

Harvard College was founded in 1636 and named after John Harvard's 1638 bequest. The 1647 Old Deluder Satan Act required larger towns to support schools so children could read Scripture. Nathaniel Ward drafted the Massachusetts Body of Liberties, adopted in 1641 as one hundred statements of rights and rules. The 1648 Laws and Liberties became New England's first printed statutory code.

sections.heading: Dissent, expansion, and royal control
paragraphs: Religious uniformity produced famous expulsions. Roger Williams was banished in 1635 and founded Providence. Anne Hutchinson and John Wheelwright challenged the ministerial establishment during the Antinomian or Free Grace Controversy; Hutchinson was banished after her 1637 civil trial and excommunicated in 1638. Thomas Hooker led settlers to Connecticut, while the Quaker Mary Dyer was executed in Boston in 1660 after repeatedly defying banishment orders.

The polity fought in the Pequot War and joined the New England Confederation in 1643. Charles II's government annulled its charter in 1684. Joseph Dudley briefly headed an interim government before Edmund Andros governed the Dominion of New England from Boston. Colonists overthrew Andros in the 1689 Boston Revolt. The 1691 charter created the Province of Massachusetts Bay, combining this polity with Plymouth and Maine under a crown-appointed governor and broader property-based voting. The 1692 Salem witch trials therefore occurred in the new royal province, not technically in the old charter colony.
